reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / Low's Clinical Autonomic Disorders
clinicalPearls: The commonest cause of transient loss of consciousness, resulting from a reflex fall in heart rate and/or blood pressure with transient global cerebral hypoperfusion
Typical triggers include prolonged standing, heat, pain, venepuncture, emotion, or the sight of blood
A prodrome of light-headedness, nausea, sweating, pallor, and visual greying usually precedes the faint, helping distinguish it from cardiac syncope and seizures
Brief myoclonic jerks (convulsive syncope) can occur and be mistaken for epilepsy
Recovery is rapid with little or no confusion, unlike the post-ictal state after a seizure
Diagnosis is clinical from a good history and eyewitness account; head-up tilt testing can support it in uncertain cases
Cardioinhibitory, vasodepressor, and mixed haemodynamic patterns are recognised
Management: education, trigger avoidance, adequate fluid and salt intake, recognising the prodrome and lying down, and physical counter-pressure manoeuvres
reference.pathophysiology: Reflex (vasovagal) syncope results from a transient, inappropriate autonomic reflex. Triggers such as prolonged standing or emotional stress lead, in susceptible people, to a paradoxical withdrawal of sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone together with a surge of vagal (parasympathetic) activity. This produces vasodilatation (the vasodepressor component) and/or bradycardia or asystole (the cardioinhibitory component), causing a sudden fall in blood pressure and transient global cerebral hypoperfusion with loss of consciousness. Because the mechanism is self-limiting and posture-dependent, lying flat restores cerebral perfusion and consciousness returns quickly. Reduced venous return from lower-body pooling and relative hypovolaemia predispose to the reflex.
additionalInvestigations: Detailed history and eyewitness account of the event and its prodrome
12-lead ECG to screen for arrhythmia or conduction disease
Lying and standing blood pressure to detect orthostatic hypotension
Head-up tilt-table testing in recurrent or uncertain cases
Ambulatory ECG or an implantable loop recorder for infrequent unexplained episodes
Echocardiography where structural heart disease is suspected
redFlags: Syncope during exertion or when supine, suggesting a cardiac cause
Absence of a prodrome, or syncope causing serious injury
Family history of sudden cardiac death or an abnormal ECG
Palpitations preceding collapse or known structural heart disease
reference.prognosis: Reflex syncope is benign in terms of mortality, but recurrent episodes can cause injury and impair quality of life; most patients respond well to education, trigger avoidance, and physical counter-manoeuvres.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing convulsive syncope as epilepsy and starting antiepileptic drugs
Failing to exclude cardiac syncope, which carries a worse prognosis
Over-relying on tilt testing, which has limited sensitivity and specificity
Not teaching counter-pressure manoeuvres and prodrome recognition
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
